l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson AP07: Testing and test plans.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Explain why testing happens at every stage and why unit testing alone is not enough. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Testing is not a single event at the end of a project but an activity that runs through the whole of development. Software is built as a set of units, so each unit is tested on its own first and any errors are corrected. Units that work perfectly in isolation may still fail when they are joined, so integration testing follows. The complete system is then tested against its agreed specification, the developer carries out a final in-house alpha phase, selected external users may beta test a pre-release version, and finally the client carries out acceptance testing before signing off the system.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Testing at every stage matters for quality because an error is far cheaper and easier to fix when it is found early, close to where it was made, than when it is discovered by the client or after the system has gone live. Testing is also planned rather than random: a test plan sets out every test, the data to use and the expected outcome, so that the most vulnerable areas, such as range limits and unusual paths through the code, are always checked. Even thorough testing cannot prove a program is free of errors.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Unit testing checks that each individual component works correctly in all circumstances. Done well, it gives confidence in each unit, which narrows the search when a fault appears later. Two approaches are used. In black-box testing the code is treated as if hidden inside a closed box: the tester knows only what the unit is meant to do, enters inputs and compares the actual outputs with the expected outputs taken from the specification.
Got it. Keep going.

Testers therefore need no knowledge of the code and can be non-technical. In white-box testing, sometimes called glass-box testing, the tester can see the code and designs tests around its structure, making sure every branch, path and loop is exercised, and concentrating on the places where errors are most likely. For example, a water-billing module that uses one rate for households and two rates for businesses has three branches; black-box tests compare bills for a range of customers, while white-box tests deliberately include at least one case for each branch and cases either side of the 100 cubic metre switch-over point. Programmers often use dry runs and trace tables when white-box testing.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Integration testing takes place when units that have already passed their own tests are combined. Faults typically occur at the interfaces between units, because one unit passes data in a form the next does not expect. A classic case is one unit storing dates as day, month, year while another reads them as month, day, year: each unit works and displays sensible dates on its own, but together they misread dates such as the fourth of July as the seventh of April. Such integration errors only appear when the parts are brought together, which is why unit testing alone is never enough.
Okay. Keep going.

When integration testing finds a fault, the unit concerned is modified, unit tested again and then re-integrated. Agreeing data formats early in a shared data dictionary reduces these problems. System testing, sometimes called application testing, is then performed on the complete, integrated system to judge whether it complies with the agreed specification. It is essentially black-box testing applied to the whole system rather than one part, so the tester does not need technical knowledge of how it was built, and it is carried out by following a detailed test plan.
Go on.

Alpha testing is the final phase of in-house testing carried out by the software developer before the software leaves their control. It brings together unit, integration and system testing, follows a test plan and may use simulated or real data; small changes can still be made afterwards. Beta testing comes after alpha testing. A pre-release version is given to a group of potential users who use it in a realistic environment, on their own equipment and without the developers present, and report any faults they find.
Right. Keep going.

It can be thought of as external user acceptance testing and is especially common for software that will be sold to many customers or run on many different devices. Acceptance testing is the final test, carried out once system testing is complete and bespoke software is ready for handover to the client. End users try it in their real working setting, with genuine data at realistic volumes, to gain confidence that it meets their requirements and works alongside the organisation’s other systems. They report problems, and once these are resolved the users sign off the software, which formally completes the contract.
Go on.

A test plan is a detailed document that a team of testers follows exactly. Its purpose is to make testing thorough and systematic, so that every requirement, every pathway through the system and every validation routine is checked, and the system’s actual performance is compared with its design. For each test the plan records a test number, the part of the system being tested, what is being tested and why (for example, boundary data to check the lowest valid value is accepted), the exact test data and the expected outcome. These columns are completed by the person who designs the tests before any testing happens.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The plan is then passed to the tester, who carries out each test and fills in the remaining columns: the actual outcome and PASS or FAIL. A test passes only when the actual outcome matches the expected outcome exactly. Failed tests are reported so the fault can be fixed, after which the tests are run again to make sure the fix works and has not broken anything else. A systems analyst may help by suggesting test data, particularly at the boundaries, and by checking results against the specification.
Go on.

Test data falls into three categories. Normal or valid data is the typical data the system expects; it is correct in type and format and should be accepted and processed. For a mark out of 100 stored as a whole number, values such as 43, 72 and 89 are normal. Boundary or extreme data is still valid but lies at the very edges of the allowed range, such as 0 and 100, because this is where programmers most often make off-by-one mistakes, for instance writing less than instead of less than or equal to.
Got it. Keep going.

Where a range is divided into bands, every band edge is a boundary, so a grading scheme of 0 to 44, 45 to 64, 65 to 79 and 80 to 100 needs tests at 0, 44, 45, 64, 65, 79, 80 and 100. Erroneous, invalid or exceptional data is wrong in type, format or range, such as 55.5, the letter X, the word sixty, a negative number or a value above the maximum. It should be rejected, ideally with a helpful message, rather than accepted or causing the program to crash. Testers often also try the values just outside each limit, which are invalid and should be rejected.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Unit testing?
Testing an individual module or subroutine on its own, usually in-house by the programmer, to check it works correctly in all circumstances.
Integration testing?
Testing units that have already been tested once they are combined, to check that they interact correctly and pass data between them as expected.
System testing?
Testing the complete, integrated system against its agreed specification; essentially black-box testing of the whole system.
Alpha testing?
The final phase of in-house testing carried out by the developer, following a test plan, before the software is released to users.
Beta testing?
Testing of a pre-release version by a group of potential external users in a realistic environment, without developers present, who report any faults.
Acceptance testing?
The final test, by end users in their real working environment with genuine data at realistic volumes, to confirm the system meets their requirements before they sign it off.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Questions on testing stages usually give one or two marks per stage, so state both what is tested and who tests it or where: unit testing is in-house by the developer on individual components; acceptance testing is by end users in a live environment with real data, ending in sign-off. Do not confuse system testing (the whole system, by the developer, against the specification) with acceptance testing (by the client, against their requirements). For alpha versus beta, contrast in-house developers with external potential users in a realistic environment. Test data questions are common and very precise. For a junior band of 4 to 12 whole years, boundary values are 4 and 12; normal is any integer strictly between; invalid examples include text or a decimal such as 7.5. When a range is open-ended, such as 13 or older, choose a reasonable upper limit and say so. Always give a specific expected outcome, such as an error message stating the valid range, never ‘it works’. A typical slip is to list 0 or 101 as boundary data that should be accepted when they lie outside the valid range.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. A games studio releases a pre-release version to 2 000 volunteer players who play at home and report bugs. This is…. Is it A, alpha testing; B, acceptance testing; C, beta testing; D, unit testing?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: beta testing. External potential users test a near-final version in a realistic environment, without developers present.
